items.stem: A student asks a chatbot how many times the letter r appears in "strawberry" and gets the wrong number. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: The word arrives as a few chunks, so the letters inside each chunk are not separate input.
options.feedback: The tokenizer cuts the word into chunks such as `str`, `aw` and `berry` before the model sees it. The model has to work out the spelling indirectly, which makes counting unreliable.

options.text: The model cannot count above two, so it loses track at the third r.
options.feedback: Counting small numbers is not the problem. The same model can count items reliably when each one arrives as its own token.

options.text: The model looks the word up in a dictionary, and the dictionary has the wrong spelling.
options.feedback: A model does not use a dictionary of spellings. It works from token numbers, and the letters inside a token are not visible to it as separate inputs.

options.text: Chatbots give rough answers on purpose, because exact answers cost more to compute.
options.feedback: Providers do charge per token, but nothing in the system gives rough answers to save money. The miscount comes from how the text is cut into tokens.

items.stem: You want a more reliable letter count from the model. Which request is most likely to work?

options.text: Ask it to write the word one letter per line, then count the r's.
options.feedback: Each letter then becomes its own token, so the model can see and count them.

options.text: Ask it to think very hard about how many r's the word has.
options.feedback: Asking for more effort does not change what the model receives. The word still arrives as chunks.

options.text: Type the word in capital letters so the letters are easier to see.
options.feedback: Capitals produce different chunks, but the letters are still grouped inside tokens.

options.text: Ask the question twice and use the answer that appears both times.
options.feedback: A second copy of the same question reaches the model in the same chunks and has the same problem.

items.stem: A company sends the same customer message to a chatbot, once in English and once in Tagalog, and is billed per token. Which result is most likely?

options.text: The Tagalog message costs more, because it is split into more tokens.
options.feedback: The tokenizer was built mostly from English text. Many Tagalog words are split into fragments, so the same meaning takes more tokens.

options.text: Both cost the same, because the meaning is the same.
options.feedback: Billing follows the number of tokens, and the meaning does not change that number.

options.text: The Tagalog message costs less, because Tagalog words are shorter.
options.feedback: Shorter words do not help if the tokenizer splits them into several pieces. Tagalog is split into more pieces, so the count goes up.

options.text: Cost depends only on the number of words in the message.
options.feedback: Providers count tokens. A word can be one token or several.

items.stem: A team pastes a long source code file into an AI assistant and hits the context window limit much sooner than the page count suggested. What best explains this?

options.text: Punctuation, operators and indentation each take tokens, so code uses more per character.
options.feedback: Code has the fewest characters per token. The window is counted in tokens, so code fills it faster.

options.text: The window is measured in pages, and a page of code holds more characters.
options.feedback: The window is measured in tokens. Pages and words are only rough conversions.

options.text: The provider charges extra for programming languages, which shrinks the limit.
options.feedback: There is no such surcharge. Code produces more tokens for the same amount of text.

options.text: The model counts every letter as a token, and code has more letters per page.
options.feedback: Tokens are chunks, often whole words in English. If every letter were a token, English text would also fill the window far faster.
